2.43.m: Sukala said: / Thus all those boars stood ready for battle; / and those hunters took their stand before the king who stood in front.
The great boar, O king of kings, having resorted to the mountain slope, / stood after forming an array with a great company of the herd.
Tawny, thick and stout-bodied, with large tusks and a huge snout, / the boar, irresistible, O king, roared most terribly.
The great king did not see those who had taken shelter in the forest of sāl and palmyra trees. / Hearing their speech, the glorious son of Manu [said]:
"Let the heroic boar be seized! Let him, haughty with power, be pierced!" / Having addressed them thus, the heroic, glorious son of Manu,
then all those hunters, intoxicated with the frenzy of hunting, / all armed and clad in armor, set out together with the dogs.
Filled with great joy, the mighty king of kings, / mounted on a horse, was accompanied by an excellent fourfold army.
He arrived at the bank of the Gaṅgā on Meru, the best of supreme mountains, / strewn with jewels and minerals, adorned with various trees.
Sukala said: / The king of mountains shines, towering extremely high with masses of rays from the abode of light, / reaching the very sky, its beauty frequented by various mountain-goers,

the lord of mountains, endowed with great splendor, its white rocky ground washed everywhere / with pure water droplets like pearls from breaking crests of waves on the bank rising up from the pure flow of the Gaṅgā many leagues wide,

surrounded by gods, Cāraṇas, and Kinnaras, by Gandharvas and Vidyādharas, / by Siddhas and hosts of Apsarases, by sages and kings of Nāgas, and Vidyā-
The mountain is adorned with śrīkhaṇḍa, abundant sandal trees, sarala pines, sāl, and tamāla trees, / with rudrākṣas and wish-fulfilling trees dense with granting excellent perfections.
Indeed, it is variegated with various minerals, and adorned with chariots / variegated with various jewels, with golden poles, and with women.
It shines with celestial coconut groves and areca-nut trees, / decorated with groves of plantains and celestial punnāga and bakula trees.
The mountain [is adorned] with campaka flowers, pāṭala trees, and ketakas, / and with canopies of various creeping plants and blooming padmakas,
and adorned with various trees bearing beautiful flowers of various colors, / crowded with divine trees and crystal rock surfaces,
with yogins, lords of yogins, and perfected ones dwelling within caves, / and the mountain [is graced] with charming cascades and numerous springs,
adorned with confluences delighted by river currents, / and with pools, ponds, and reservoirs holding pure water.
The king of mountains shines solitary, together with the peaks situated [upon it], / adorned with herds of deer, with śarabhas, and with tigers,
and always with greatly intoxicated elephants and large buffalos; / through numerous divine aspects that king of mountains shines.
The heroic ruler of Ayodhyā, Ikṣvāku, the joy of Manu, / accompanied by that good wife and with his fourfold army,
The hunters and the swift-running dogs go ahead / to where the heroic, powerful boar stays with his wife,
guarded by many boars, by elders and by young ones, / having resorted to the ground of Meru, along the banks of the Gaṅgā on all sides.
Sukala said: / Filled with joy, the boar spoke to that very beloved [wife]: / "O beloved, look: the mighty ruler of Kośala has arrived!"
The very wise king plays at hunting, aiming at me. / I will indeed fight a battle that will gladden gods and demons!
Then the king of great majesty, with bow in hand holding an arrow, / spoke, full of joy, to Sudevā, whose body was true virtue:
"Behold, my beloved, the mighty boar, roaring, possessed of great strength, / surrounded by his herd, unbearable to the hunters of game.
This very day, my love, I shall slay him with sharp, fine arrows! / For that mighty hero will surely advance against me in battle."
Having spoken thus to his beloved wife, the fond king addressed the hunters: / "O great heroes, launch [an attack on] the boar just as a hero [would]!"
Then those heroes were dispatched, endowed with strength, majesty, and valor; / roaring and running forth, endowed with strength, majesty, and valor,
all went toward the boar with the speed of the wind at that moment; / those forest-dwellers pierced him with nets of sharp arrows,
and with diverse weapons and missiles, [assailing] the boar who possessed a heroic form.

Sukala said: / As dense rainclouds shower upon a mountain, so fell the arrows and javelins loosed by the hunters across the ground; / struck and then overcome by hundreds of forceful strikers, the boar, protector of the herd, entered the fight.

With his sons, grandsons, and kin, he destroyed the enemies; struck down by his tusk in battle, the hunters fell; / feet and hands fell from his whirl of speed as he stood, and the boar saw that roaring hunter who had come forth.
Destroyed by his own radiance, struck down by the tusk at the tip of his snout, / he went where the king stood, and he desired a duel [with him].

Violently terrifying the great lord of the Ikṣvākus, that furious lord of boars / desired to fight with that Ikṣvāku in the forest, filled with joy for battle.

The boar, skilled in battle, once more desired combat, agitating the earth in fury with the tip of his snout, with his very sharp teeth and claws,

Out of pride in uttering his roar, he struck that pure ruler of the earth; and the king, the son of Manu, his hair bristling with joy upon recognizing the valor of Viṣṇu,

having seen the matchless virility of the boar, thought, "Is this a lord, or a great boar?" considering in his mind that it was the enemy of the gods suddenly in the form of a boar,
Seeing the elephant-army of great power brought together swiftly in great abundance to destroy the boar, [he ordered,] "Quickly seize him, seize him!"

Elephants and very swift chariots were dispatched, along with [soldiers] bearing fine arrows, swords, bhuśuṇḍi-missiles, and clubs, / and roaring hunters with nooses in hand intent upon him; unchecked, they did not halt wherever horses and elephants advanced.
Here and there he was not seen; here and there he was seen; in some places he displayed terror, in some places he crushed the horses.
Having crushed the brave warriors, the boar, invincible in battle, / his eyes red with fury, uttered a ferocious roar.
Seeing that colossal creature fighting, invincible in battle, / unleashing a sound like a thundercloud, the heroic ruler of Kośala,
firmly roared, roamed the battle, and triumphed over the warriors by his own radiance; / the tusk in his mouth gleamed and flashed like lightning.
The son of Manu, having seen the boar pierced one by one with sharp arrows / and struck by weapons along with his kin,
the king said: "Why do the brave warriors of the army not seize him here by their might? / Fight there with sharp arrows, with sharp [weapons], and even with this [bow]!"
Having heard that command of the noble king, even though he was enraged, / all those soldiers then stood ready for battle.
Surrounding that boar who stood for battle in the forest on all sides / with many thousands of warriors, they pierced him in the fight.

Pierced then by several great warriors with nets of arrows on the battlefield, / struck here with strikes of discs, and there with blows like thunderbolts, that invincible one was struck by great [heroes] in the fight.
Then, filled with rage at his feats, that boar completely severed the nooses and set out in battle; / he advanced along with the great boars, anointed with streams of blood.
The hero struck with his snout, and the hero slashed horses and elephants; / with the sharp tip of his tusk, he cast down heroic foot-soldiers in his wrathful state.
Enraged, he severed the trunk of an elephant, and delighted, [crushed] fallen warriors with the claws of his feet.
Then all those boars and hunters fought one another, / engaging in combat with eyes red with fury.
Boars were killed by hunters, and good hunters were killed by boars; / struck down, they fell on the ground, crimson with blood.
Quitting life, the hunters fell in battle, killed by the boars; / boars died there, and dogs lost their lives.
Everywhere the slayers of game fell dead upon the ground; / many boars were felled by the blows of the king's sword.
O best of kings, how many terrified boars perished, were killed, or took refuge in strongholds, / in thickets, inside clefts, and inside caves!
Some hunters died, rent by the boars with the tips of their tusks; / torn to pieces, having given up their breath, they went to heaven.
Snares, nets of nooses, traps, cages, / and sinews fell upon the ground everywhere on every side.
One boar stood firm along with his beloved / and five or seven grandsons, proud of his strength, ready to fight.
Then the sow spoke again to that beloved boar: / "Go, my love, together with me and with these little ones!"
Affectionately the boar said to his troubled, dearly beloved [mate]: / "Where shall I go, broken? There is no place [for me] on the surface of the earth.
If I am destroyed, O noble one, the herd of boars will perish. / Between two lions, a boar drinks water;
between two boars, a lion does not drink water at all. / Such supreme strength is seen among the breed of boars.
I would surely destroy that if I were to go away broken. / I know dharma, O noble one, which produces abundant welfare.
Why should a fighter perish out of greed or fear? / Abandoning the sacred ford of battle, he would become a sinner, beyond doubt.
Seeing a sharp array of weapons, one attains delight; / plunging into the immortal river, one reaches the opposite shore of the sacred ford.
He goes to the realm of Viṣṇu and redeems his ancestors. / How then could I flee, broken, from what is approaching?
When one rejoices at the sight of a battle crowded with weapons, which brings delight to great heroes, / listen to the fruit of his merit:
At every step, there arises the great merit of bathing in the Bhāgīrathī. / But he who flees from battle and goes home out of greed, listen, my love:
He reveals his mother's flaw; he is declared to have been born a woman. / Here are sacrifices and sacred fords; here are the gods of great splendor;
sages, Siddhas, and Cāraṇas watch the spectacle, my dear; / the three worlds abide right there where a hero's valor is displayed."
All the inhabitants of the three worlds look upon one fleeing from battle; / they curse that pitiless, sinful coward and laugh at him again and again.
Dharmarāja will surely reveal a wretched destiny to him, without doubt. / Facing the foe in the struggle of battle, he might drink the blood from his own head;
he enjoys the fruit of an aśvamedha and goes to the world of Indra. / When a hero conquers his enemies in battle, O fair-faced woman,
then he enjoys royal fortune and various pleasures, without a doubt. / When he abandons his life there, facing forward and helpless,
he goes to the highest abode and enjoys a divine maiden. / Thus I know the dharma: how could I retreat broken?
I will fight in battle with this one, of this there is no doubt— / with the steadfast King Ikṣvāku, the son of Manu.
Take the young ones and go; live happily, O fair-faced woman!" / Hearing his words, she said: "I am bound by your bonds,
by love, pride, affection, and amorous play, O dear one! / In your presence, together with our sons, I will give up my life, O giver of honor."
Having spoken thus to each other, wishing each other's welfare, / resolved on battle, they both looked upon their enemies,
[namely,] the heroic king of Kośala, the wise Ikṣvāku.

Just as a cloud roars aloud in the sky during the rainy seasons with flashes of lightning, / even so he roared together with his beloved, and challenged the foremost of kings with the tips of his hooves.
The noble king saw that single boar roaring, full of prowess; / that steadfast hero among men, endowed with the speed of his horse, rode straight out to face him.

2.44.m: Sukala said: / Seeing his difficult-to-withstand army conquered by that unyielding one, / the king became furious against the cruel, unbearable boar.
Quickly seizing his bow and an arrow like the fire of cosmic destruction, / he rode straight toward him on his horse.
When that leader of the herd of boars saw the king mounted on horseback, endowed with supreme prowess, a slayer of foes, / he advanced forward on the battleground to confront him.
Indeed, when struck by a sharp arrow, he fell beneath the king's horse's feet; / but leaping over him right there with a swift mind, the excellent boar charged with vehement speed.
The horse, injured by the boar, was pierced in its gait and could not move on the earth; / struck by the snout, the horse fell to the ground, and the king quickly mounted his chariot.
He indeed roared with the grunts of the boar kind; then with great speed, / the leader of the herd in the midst of battle was struck with a mace by the king of Kośala situated on his chariot.
Then, abandoning his own body, he truly went to the supreme abode of Hari.
Indeed, having fought in battle with the well-intentioned king, / when that king of kings among boars was slain and fell upon the ground, the foremost gods rained down beautiful flowers.
A pile of flowers arose over him, fragrant as if from celestial trees, / and the gods, fully delighted, poured a rain of saffron and sandalwood.
While being touched by that benevolent king, he became four-armed, O king, / clad in divine garments, possessing divine ornaments and form, shining with his own splendor like the sun.
When he went to heaven in a celestial vehicle, honored by the king of the gods and the deities, / having cast off his previous body right here, he became the king of the Gandharvas once again.

2.45.m: Sukala said: / Then all those hunters went toward the sow; / brave, fierce, and dreadful, they arrived with nooses in hand.
And keeping her four young ones near, the sow stood, / having seen her beloved slain along with his family in the great battle.
"What my husband contemplated has been attained, and he has been honored by sages and gods; / that noble one has gone to heaven by means of this valorous deed.
By this path I too shall go to heaven where my husband dwells." / Having firmly resolved thus, she thought about her sons:
"If these four children of mine, the sustainers of the lineage, survive, / it will ensure the continuation of this brave and noble boar.
By what means can I ensure the protection of my sons?" / Being full of such worry, she saw a mountain pass;
a wide path there led to an exit. / Having firmly resolved thus, she thought about her sons.
She said to those bewildered sons, O great king: / "As long as I stand here, O sons, go quickly!"
Among them, the eldest son [said]: "How shall I go, O mother, / abandoning you out of craving for life? Shame on my life, O mother!
I will pursue my father's enmity and vanquish the foes in battle. / You take my three younger brothers to the rugged mountain cave.
Whoever goes away abandoning father and mother is evil-minded, / and surely goes to hell, which is teeming with millions of worms."
Afflicted with great sorrow, she said to him: "How could I abandon you, O son, / and depart, I great sinner? Let the [other] three sons go!"
The three younger ones went into the mountain forest, / while the two of them went to the battlefield right before their eyes,
roaring again and again with fiery vigor and great strength. / Then those heroic hunters arrived, swift as the wind.
Those three were sent along that difficult path, O king, / while these two, mother and son, stood blocking the way.
Then the hunters arrived, holding swords, arrows, and bows; / they struck with sharp lances, with discuses, and then with clubs.
Keeping his mother behind him, the son fought with them; / some were slain by his tusks, and some were struck down with his snout.
He struck with the tips of his hooves, and warriors fell in battle. / The boar fought in combat and was observed by the noble king.
Knowing that this one was even braver than his father, he advanced to face him, / bow in hand, the glorious and majestic son of Manu.
Pierced in the chest with a sharp arrow resembling a crescent moon / shot by the noble king, he fell to the earth struck down.
He died instantly; the boar fell to the ground. / Falling into supreme distress for her son, she herself went over to him.
And heroic fighters were slain by her with blows of her snout on the surface of the earth; / heroic hunters fell down—how many were destroyed and killed, O king!
Routing the great army with her tusks, the sow then seemed / like a spirit of destruction that had arisen, producing great terror.
Then the queen said to him, who resembled the son of the king of the gods: / "O king, your great army is truly being destroyed by this one!
Why do you overlook her, O dear one? Tell me the reason for that!" / The great king said to her: "I will not kill this female.
A great fault is seen by the gods, O dear one, in killing a female; / therefore, one should not slay a female, nor will I dispatch anyone [to do so].
I fear the sin arising from killing her, O beautiful woman." / Having spoken thus, the king, the lord of the earth, desisted.
A hunter named Jhārjhara saw that sow / causing slaughter among them, unbearable even for excellent warriors.
He pierced [her] with great speed with a sharp arrow; / pierced by that arrow, drenched with blood,
shining, having attained swiftness, agitated with heroic majesty, / Jhārjhara was struck in battle by her snout in return.
Struck then by that falling Jhārjhara / with a sharp sword, she fell, torn apart.
Panting on the battlefield, overcome with fainting, / seized by great agony, she remained alive on the surface of the earth.

2.46.m: Sukala said: / Seeing the panting sow fallen, who was affectionate to her offspring, / Sudevā, filled with compassion, went toward that suffering one,
sprinkling her face with cool water / and then her entire body, the afflicted one who had shone in battle.
With auspicious, cool water, she spoke to the one who was sprinkling her; / she spoke human speech in a melodious voice to the king's beloved:
"May there be happiness for you, O queen, since I have been sprinkled by you; / by your contact and by your sight, the heap of my sins has vanished."
Hearing that remarkable speech possessed of a wondrous form, / [Sudevā thought:] 'Wondrous is this which has been seen by me, and your speech brings freedom from affliction.
And although belonging to the animal species, she speaks with excellence clearly, / endowed with vowels and consonants, speaking excellent Sanskrit to me.'
With joy and also with wonder, performing an excellent act of courage, / the fortunate lady, standing there, spoke these words to her husband:
"Look, O King, this extraordinary [creature] speaks great Sanskrit, / though born in an animal womb, just as a human being would speak!"
Hearing that, the king, the best among all who possess knowledge, / [said,] 'Wondrous is this wondrous form, such as has not been seen or heard by me!'
Then the king said to his dear Sudevā at that time: / 'Ask this auspicious one, my beloved, who she might be.'
Hearing the king's words, she questioned the sow: / 'Who might you be, O auspicious one? Much about you appears wondrous.
Born in an animal womb, you truly utter human speech, / filled with excellence and wisdom. Tell me of your previous deeds,
and also of your husband, O noble lady—this great-souled warrior. / What dharma was this, of great valor, that he has gone to heaven through heroic deeds?
Tell everything concerning the previous lives of yourself and your husband.' / Having spoken thus, the fortunate beloved of the king became silent.
The sow said: / 'If you ask me, O auspicious one, concerning myself and this great-souled one, / I shall tell you all about our conduct and past deeds.
This one was a very wise Gandharva, learned in singing, / named Raṅgavidyādhara, skilled in the meaning of all sacred treatises.
Resorting to Meru, the best of supreme mountains, / with lovely caves and waterfalls, the eminent sage Pulastya of great splendor
practiced austerities, glorious with a sincere mind. / That Vidyādhara went there of his own will, O great lord.
Resorting to that best of mountains, he practiced singing at that time, / endowed with notes and rhythm, melodious, O lady of lovely smiles!
Hearing the song, the sage's mind was distracted from meditation. / He spoke thus to that singing song-expert Vidyādhara:
"By your celestial song, the gods become infatuated, no doubt, / with its melodious sound, most auspicious, and rhythmic measure, O learned one,
with an expression united with tempo and accompanied by modulations; / my mind has been moved from meditation by this song, O you of good vows!
Abandon this place and go to another place." / The song-expert Vidyādhara said: "Song is equal to knowledge of the Self; why should I go to another place?
It causes grief to no one; it always gives happiness to mortals. / By this celestial song all deities are pleased.
Even Śambhu is brought here, delighted by the sound of song, O twice-born one! / Song is declared to contain all aesthetic sentiments; song is the giver of bliss.
All aesthetic sentiments such as the erotic are established through song; / the four supreme Vedas attain beauty through song.
Through song all deities attain satisfaction, not otherwise. / Yet you thus censure song, and would thus drive me away!
This injustice, O fortunate one, is seen on your part alone." / Pulastya said: "What you have said today is true: the meaning of song grants much merit.
Listen to my words; abandon pride, O highly intelligent one! / I do not revile song; I revere song, not otherwise.
These fourteen branches of knowledge, conferring understanding through single-mindedness, / attain perfection for living beings with an unmoving mind.
Austerity and likewise mantras are perfected by one-pointed thought. / The great group of sense organs is fickle, according to my view;
it leads the self forcefully toward all sense objects, / having shaken the mind away from meditation, without doubt.
Where there is no sound, no form, and no young woman, / there sages go for the perfection of austerity.
This song of yours is holy, conferring much happiness; / we who dwell in the forest may not look upon it, O heroic one!
Go to another place, or else we shall depart." / The song-expert Vidyādhara said: "He by whom the power and group of sense organs is conquered, that great soul,
he is called a victorious yogin; he is a hero, he is a spiritual practitioner. / Having heard a sound or having seen a form in this way, O highly intelligent one,
he who does not waver from meditation is a steadfast practitioner of austerity. / But you are lacking in power, since you are conquered by the senses.
Even in heaven there is no capacity to overpower my song. / All those who lack vigor shun the forest, without doubt.
This forest region is common, O Brahmin, without doubt, / to the gods and to all living beings, just as for me, so for you.
How can I go, abandoning such an unsurpassed forest? / You may go or you may stay; what is destined will not be otherwise."
The song-expert Vidyādhara spoke thus to that Brahmin then. / Having heard his reply, by that sage
the wise one reflected: 'By doing what would good be done?' / Practicing forbearance, the best of the twice-born then went to another place.
The righteous-minded one practiced austerity, seated always in a yogic posture, / abandoning desire, anger, delusion, and likewise greed,
restraining all the senses along with the mind. / Thus remained the yogin, Pulastya, the best among sages.
Sukala said: / When that fortunate one, Pulastya, the eminent sage, had departed, / directed by destiny, that song-expert Vidyādhara
thought for a very long time: 'He has not been seen [here] out of fear of me; / where has he gone, or where does he stay, and what is he doing, and how?'
Knowing the son of the Lotus-born to be dwelling in a solitary forest, / he went in the form of a boar to his unsurpassed hermitage.
Seeing that great soul seated on his mat, enveloped in flames of ascetic energy, / he caused agitation to that Brahmin, O beautiful lady!
He harassed the Brahmin continually with the tip of his snout through wicked actions; / knowing him to be an animal, O king, he endured his evil deed.
He would urinate in front [of him] and then drop excrement; / he would dance and play there, fall down, and jump up again.
Knowing him to be a beast, the sage ignored him, O king. / But once he arrived again in that form,
and then laughed with boisterous laughter; / he wept there, and sang a song in a sweet voice.
The brāhmaṇa, seeing that Vidyādhara of song arrived thus / and witnessing his antics, [thought:] 'This is certainly no boar.
Having understood his behaviour, [I see] he is trying to disturb me thus. / Knowing him to be a beast, he was disregarded by me, [yet] this wicked one is utterly shameless.'
Recognising that great being to be merely a vile Gandharva, / the tiger among sages was enraged, and of great intellect, cursed him:
'Since you try to disturb me in the form of a boar, / therefore, O great sinner, go into the sinful womb of a boar!'
Cursed by that brāhmaṇa, he went to the god Puraṃdara / and, trembling, said to that great being, O fair-faced one:
'Hear [my] words, O thousand-eyed one! Your task was performed by me. / While that bull among sages was performing harsh austerities,
he was disturbed and agitated by me from the power of those austerities. / I was cursed by that brāhmaṇa, and my divine form was destroyed.
Rescue me thus, O Śakra, from having fallen into the womb of a beast!' / Having understood the situation of that Vidyādhara of song,
Indra went with him and addressed that sage: / 'Let grace be granted, O lord! You know [all] accomplishment, O best of the twice-born.
Let this one be forgiven, O best of sages, and release from the curse be granted!' / Beseeched thus by Mahendra, the brāhmaṇa of pleased mind said:
Pulastya said: / 'At your word, O lord of the gods, he must indeed be forgiven by me. / There will be a great king of great might, the son of Manu,
named Ikṣvāku, righteous-souled and guardian of all duties. / When death comes to this [creature] at his hands,
then he will indeed regain his own body; there is no doubt in this.' / All this account of the boar has been related to you.
Now I shall tell you of myself; listen, along with your husband, / to the terrible sin committed formerly by sinful me.

2.47.m: Sukalā said: / Sudevā of lovely limbs then said to that female boar: / 'Having entered the womb of a beast, how is it that you speak Sanskrit?
Tell me, whence has such great knowledge arisen [in you]? / How do you know the life of your husband and of yourself, O fair one?'
The female boar said: / 'Possessed by the condition of a beast, I was robbed [of awareness] by delusion, O fair-complexioned lady; / struck down by swords and arrows, I fell at the front of battle.
Overcome by fainting and devoid of consciousness, O fair-faced one, / I was sprinkled by you, O beautiful lady, with a holy hand.
When my body was sprinkled with cold holy water / from your hand, delusion left me and vanished.
Just as darkness goes to destruction before bright rays of light, / so by your sprinkling did my sin depart, O fair one.
By your grace, O lovely-limbed lady, ancient knowledge was regained; / and I have come to know, O fair one, that I shall go to a holy destination.
Listen, I shall recount my former history, / and the great evil done by sinful me, O auspicious lady.
In the great country called Kaliṅga, there was a city named Śrīpura, / filled with all perfections and inhabited by the four castes.
There lived a certain brāhmaṇa known as Vasudatta, / ever devoted to the conduct of Brahmā and dedicated to truth and dharma,
a knower of the Veda, a knower of spiritual knowledge, pure, virtuous, wealthy, / abounding in wealth and grain, adorned with sons and grandsons.
I was his daughter, O auspicious lady, adored by brothers, kin, and relatives, / and adorned with ornaments and fine dress, O fair-faced one.
That noble-minded father gave me the name Sudevā; / I was always the darling of him, my father, O great-minded lady.
I was peerless in beauty; there was none like me in the world. / Intoxicated with pride in beauty and youth, with a lovely smile,
I was a maiden of great beauty, shining with all ornaments. / Seeing me, all the people and the gathering of kin
sought me in this way for marriage, O fair-faced one. / Though I was asked for by all the brāhmaṇas, my father would not give me away.
Out of affection, O fortunate one, that noble-minded man was infatuated; / so I was not given away then by that great-souled father.
Youth arrived, O lady, endowed with longing in me. / Seeing such beauty of mine, my mother was exceedingly distressed.
Then she said to my father: 'Why is the maiden not given away? / To what good brāhmaṇa, a great-souled brāhmaṇa,
will you give the girl, O fortunate one? For she has attained her youth.' / Vasudatta, the foremost of the twice-born, the best of brāhmaṇas, replied
to my mother: 'O fortunate lady, listen to my words! / I am bewildered with great attachment to my daughter, O fair-complexioned one.
Listen, O fair one: whichever brāhmaṇa will become a resident of my house, / to him I shall give the maiden as a son-in-law, no doubt.
For she, Sudevā, is dearer than my life, there is no doubt.' / Thus my father Vasudatta spoke concerning me.
Born in the family of Kuśika, skilled in all sciences, / endowed with the virtues of brāhmaṇas, well-behaved, virtuous, pure,
accomplished in the study of the Veda, reciting in a sweet voice, / there came to the door for alms [a youth] bereft of father and mother.
Seeing him arrived and beholding his handsome form, the wise / father spoke thus to him: 'Who may you be?
What is your name, family, lineage, and conduct? Tell me now.' / Hearing the father's words, he said to Vasudatta:
'I was born in the lineage of Kuśika, a master of the Veda and the Vedāṅgas; / my name is Śivaśarman, and I am bereft of father and mother.
I have four other brothers, all masters of the Veda. / Thus my family is described, and my conduct conforms to the family.'
When all was thus explained to the father by Śivaśarman, / at an auspicious lagna and tithi, when the lunar mansion sacred to Bhaga arrived,
I was given away by my father to that brāhmaṇa, O fortunate one. / I resided in my father's house alone, together with that great-souled man.
My husband was never attended upon by sinful me then, / for I was utterly deluded by pride and the abundant wealth of my parents.
Massaging of his limbs was never done by me, / neither with loving passion, affection, nor pleasant words, O fair one.
He was always viewed with cruel thoughts by sinful me; / through association with unchaste women, I fell into their disposition, O fair one.
I did not act for the welfare of my parents, my husband, or my brothers, / wherever I went.
Seeing my bad conduct thus, my husband Śivaśarman, / out of affection for the family of his in-laws, that wise husband of mine,
said nothing to me, and he tolerated my bad conduct. / Though restrained by my family, I was utterly sinful in this manner.
Knowing his good character and the righteousness of Śivaśarman, / my father and my mother were all grieved by my sin.
Seeing my evil deed, my husband departed outside from his own house; / leaving behind that land and this village, he went away from there.
When my husband had gone, my father was overcome with worry, / his soul grieved by my grief, like one afflicted with disease.
My mother spoke to him, her husband afflicted with grief: / 'Why are you worrying, my beloved? Speak your sorrow before me.'
Vasudatta said to her, my mother, O delight: / 'Leaving his daughter behind, the brāhmaṇa, our son-in-law, has gone, listen, dear wife.
She is of sinful conduct, merciless, walking in sin; / for Śivaśarman, the high-minded, was abandoned by her.
Out of courtesy toward the entire family, the high-minded one, / that good twice-born, my dear, never spoke harshly to Sudevā.
He lives with a gentle disposition, nor does he blame or censure / Sudevā of sinful conduct; he is indeed a learned, wise man.
This wicked Sudevā will certainly become the destroyer of the family; / abandoning her, I shall go away, O dweller of the house.'
The brāhmaṇa woman said: 'Only today have you recognized your daughter’s faults, my beloved? / By your delusion and fond affection she was ruined; listen now.
One should indulge a son only as long as he is five years old; / with a mind bent on discipline, my beloved, one should constantly foster him without delusion.
Through bathing, clothing, chewable food, meals, and drinks, without doubt, / a father should yoke that son to virtues, my beloved, and to good learning.
For the sake of teaching virtues, a father should always be free from delusion; / in rearing and nourishing, my beloved, excessive attachment arises.
One should not tell a son he has virtues; one should censure him day by day, / and speak harshly to him continually, tormenting him with words,
So that he, intent on knowledge, may constantly master good learning, / even under the pretext of pride, abandoning sin from afar.
Expertise is constantly produced in sciences and in virtues. / A mother should strike her daughter, and a mother-in-law should strike her daughter-in-law;
A guru should strike a student; then they attain success, not otherwise. / A husband should strike his wife, my beloved, and a king his minister in the same way;
A wise man should strike a horse, and a driver an elephant day by day. / With a mind bent on discipline, they achieve success through chastisement and protection, O lord.
By you she was ruined, O lord, continually and without doubt, / as well as along with that good brāhmaṇa, Śivaśarman.
She was made unchecked in the house; thereby she was ruined, O wise one. / One should keep an unmarried girl in the house only so long, beloved; hear my words:
Only as long as she is eight years old; one should not keep her once she is grown. / Whatever sin a daughter commits while dwelling in her father's house,
Both parents incur that sin. / Therefore, a capable [grown] girl should not be kept in one's own dwelling.
To whomever she is given, in his house she should be nurtured; / staying there, she should attend upon her beloved husband, endowed with virtues, with devotion.
Fame accrues to the family; the father lives in happiness. / If she commits sin while staying there, the husband consumes that sin.
Dwelling there, she ever flourishes with sons and grandsons; / the father attains fame through the good virtues of his daughter, my dear.
Therefore, my beloved, one should not keep a married daughter in the house. / In this regard, beloved, an ancient story will be heard, which will take place
When the twenty-eighth Dvāpara age arrives, O lord, / regarding the heroic Ugrasena, the eldest of the Yadus, the great [king].
I shall relate his deed to you; listen with a single mind, O twice-born!'

2.48.m: The brāhmaṇa woman said: 'In the lovely region of Mathurā, in Mathurā, there was an excellent king, / renowned as Ugrasena, a Yādava who slew enemy warriors.
He knew the truth of all dharma and wealth; he knew the Vedas; he was learned, mighty, / generous, enjoying [life], appreciating virtue; that king recognized true virtues.
The wise king ruled his kingdom and protected the subjects according to dharma. / Thus was that mighty Ugrasena of great splendor.
In the sacred region of Vidarbha, there was the powerful Satyaketu; / his daughter was highly fortunate, lotus-eyed, with a lotus face,
Known by name as Padmāvatī, devoted to truth and dharma; / endowed with the virtues of women, she was like a second ocean-born goddess [Lakṣmī].
The princess of Vidarbha shone, O king, with her own virtues based on truth. / But Ugrasena of Mathurā married that beautiful-eyed lady.
Together with her, that powerful and highly fortunate king rejoiced happily; / exceedingly delighted with her virtues, he became happy in her company.
The lord of Mathurā was captivated by affection and love for her; / the highly fortunate Padmāvatī became dearer to him than life.
Without her he would not eat; with her he would sport; / without her he would never indulge in the highest pleasure.
Thus they became mutually delightful and unsurpassed, / full of affection, bestowing happiness and great joy, O best of the twice-born.
Then King Satyaketu remembered Padmāvatī, / his own daughter; and the highly fortunate mother of hers was deeply grieved.
The king of Vidarbha dispatched messengers to Mathurā, / to Ugrasena, the foremost heroic king of men, respectfully, O best of the twice-born.
The messenger addressed words to the great king Ugrasena, / gladdening him with devotion and affection: 'The heroic ruler of Vidarbha
Reports his own welfare and inquires after yours. / The great king Satyaketu has asked this of you:
"Send my daughter Padmāvatī here to see me. / If you, O lord, hold regard for affection, love, and what is dear to him,
Please send that highly fortunate woman, your beloved who brings delight; / the great king remains filled with longing and eagerness."
Having heard that message, Ugrasena, the best of kings, / out of love and affection for that high-souled Satyaketu,
And out of courtesy, O foremost of the twice-born, the powerful King Ugrasena / sent away his beloved wife Padmāvatī.
Sent by him, O king of kings, that chaste Padmāvatī went to her / former house, filled with great joy.
The lovely and auspicious lady saw her family beginning with her father; / then, devoted to truth, she bowed her head at her father's feet.
When Padmāvatī arrived, O best of the twice-born, the great king, / the ruler of Vidarbha, was filled with tremendous joy.
Magnified with gifts, honors, garments, and ornaments, / Padmāvatī dwelt happily in her father's house.
Together with her female companions, she moved about without hesitation; / she amused herself there just as she had before,
In the house, in the forest, by the ponds, and likewise in the palace. / Having become like a young girl again, she behaved without modesty.
She moved about without hesitation, O twice-born, always with her female friends, / a highly fortunate devoted wife filled with great joy.
'The happiness of one's father's house is difficult to obtain in the father-in-law's house'— / knowing this, she amused herself then: 'When will it ever be like this [again]?'
With this disposition of delusion, eager for play, the fair-faced lady / was constantly with her female companions in the forests and pleasure gardens.

2.49.m: The brāhmaṇa woman said: 'Once, the highly fortunate lady went to an excellent mountain, / having seen a delightful forest adorned with plantain groves.
with śāla, tāla, and tamāla trees, and with towering coconut trees, / with betel-nut fruits, citrons, oranges, and lovely rose-apples,
with campaka and pāṭala blossoms, holy and blooming, with kuṭakas and banyans, / endowed with aśoka and bakula trees, adorned with diverse trees.
That sacred mountain with the best of blossoming trees, / filled with various minerals, was seen everywhere as charming.
The lake was auspicious on all sides, filled with holy water, / with blooming lotuses and others, fragrant golden water-lilies,
Shining with white water-lilies, with well-blossomed red water-lilies, / with blue water-lilies and white lotuses, and with swans and water fowls,
with aquatic birds and others, rich in various minerals; / the lake was bright all around, filled with flocks of various birds.
It was embellished by the holy and sweet-toned cries of cuckoos; / by the sweet sounds it echoed sweetly everywhere.
It was beautiful on all sides with the pleasant hum of six-footed bees. / Such a charming mountain and that most excellent forest,
and the lake auspicious on all sides, the king's daughter beheld; / sporting then in the company of her female friends, that princess of Vidarbha,
beholding the sacred forest filled with flowers everywhere, / out of restlessness, playful power, feminine nature, and sportiveness,
Padmāvatī then, on the shore of the lake with her companions, / absorbed in water-sports, laughed and sang in turn.
Sporting in that lake, that passionate lady / would pass her time happily then, O brāhmaṇa.
Viṣṇu said: / There was a Daitya named Gobhila, a servant of Vaiśravaṇa; / borne along in a celestial aerial car, immersed in every enjoyment,
Gobhila, the foremost of Daityas, was traveling along the path of the sky. / By him that large-eyed princess of Vidarbha was then seen fearless.
She was the best among all women, the beloved wife of Ugrasena; / peerless in the world for her beauty, she shone in all her limbs.
“Is she Rati, the wife of Love, or is she the beloved of Hari, / or could she be Goddess Pārvatī, or might she be Śacī?
Such as she appears, the foremost and best among women, / there is no second like her on the orb of the earth.
As the full moon shines beautiful among the lunar mansions, / so does this fair-faced woman shine with virtues, beauty, and arts.
As a swan among lotuses, so is this sweet-smiling woman. / Ah, what beauty! Ah, what grace is seen in her!
Who is she, and whose is this beautiful maiden with lovely, rounded breasts?” / Thus pondered the Daitya Gobhila regarding the fair-faced Padmāvatī.
Having reflected for a moment, O brāhmaṇa, [wondering] “Whose can she be?”, / he learned through his great insight that she was indeed the princess of Vidarbha, without a doubt:
“The beloved of Ugrasena, devoted to the vow of fidelity to her husband, / standing firm by her own moral power, unattainable even to men.
Ugrasena is a great fool, by whom this maiden was sent away / to her father's house; he is indeed deprived of good fortune!
Without her, how could that rogue ever live? / Or is the king impotent, that he should abandon her?
Seeing her, his heart became filled with lust that very moment: / “This maiden is devoted to her husband, difficult to be attained by men.
How shall I go and enjoy her? Passion afflicts me exceedingly. / If I depart without enjoying her, it will surely be my death,
this very day, no doubt, since lust has immense power.” / Having become full of anxiety thus, Gobhila reflected in his mind.
Assuming an illusory form of King Ugrasena— / exactly as King Ugrasena was, with all his limbs and features,
Gobhila became just like him in gait, voice, and speech, / with the same garments, the same attire, and also of the same age,
wearing celestial garlands and garments, anointed with celestial fragrant ointments, / his body adorned with all ornaments, just like the lord of Mathurā.
Having thus become just like him, transformed into Ugrasena, that Daitya, / endowed with supreme illusion and with an abundance of beauty and charm,
took his stand on the mountain peak, resorting to the shade of an aśoka tree. / Seated upon a slab of stone, that wicked-minded hero held the neck of a lute.
Singing in a sweet voice a song that would enchant the universe, / accompanied by beat, measure, and rhythm, adorned with the seven notes,
the evil-minded one sang the song, bewitched by her beauty. / He stood on the mountain peak, O brāhmaṇa, filled with great joy.
Remaining in the midst of her female friends, that fair-faced Padmāvatī / heard the sweet-sounding song, endowed with rhythm, measure, and tempo.
“Who is this righteous person singing, conferring great happiness, / a song accompanied by proper performance and endowed with all sentiments?”
Going with her companions out of curiosity, the king's daughter / [approached] the spotless, beautiful stone slab in the shade of the aśoka tree,
and beheld the vile Dānava Gobhila in the guise of the king, / wearing a garland of flowers and robes, anointed with heavenly fragrance,
his limbs adorned with all ornaments. The chaste Padmāvatī [thought]: / “When did the lord of Mathurā, devoted to dharma, arrive?
My noble lord indeed, leaving his kingdom far away!” / While she was still pondering, that sinner
called out to her eagerly: “Come here, O my beloved!” / Startled and apprehensive, she [wondered], “How has my husband arrived?”
Embarrassed and distressed, she then cast down her face: / “Sinful and wicked-mannered as I am, I have wandered about without hesitation.
This noble lord will surely be angry, there is no doubt.” / While she was still reflecting thus, by that sinner
she was called out eagerly: “Come, come, O my beloved! / Deprived of you, O goddess, O fair-faced one, to sustain my life-breaths
I am not able, O beloved! My life is dear [only through you]. / Greedy for your love, I cannot bear to be separated from you.”
The brāhmaṇa woman said: / Being spoken to thus, she went and looked upon his handsome face with modesty. / Then the Daitya, embracing the chaste Padmāvatī,
led her to a secluded place and enjoyed her according to his desire. / Then, by the Daitya Gobhila, the daughter of Satyaketu
Sukala said: / [was violated]. Finding no mark on his scrotum, the fair-faced woman, / grasping her garment, became apprehensive and grieved.
Full of wrath, she spoke words to the vile Dānava Gobhila: / “Who are you, evil-behaved, merciless one in the form of a Dānava?
Desiring to curse him, preparing herself, her eyes troubled with grief, / trembling then, O king, oppressed by a burden of sorrow:
“Approaching under the guise of my beloved, O evil-minded one, / you have destroyed my foremost duty, my unsurpassed fidelity to my husband!
Weeping in a loud voice [she cried]: “My life has been ruined by you! / See my power right here; I shall pronounce a terrible curse!”
Speaking thus, desiring to curse that Gobhila—

2.50.m: Sukala said: / Hearing her words, Gobhila spoke these words: / “You wish to curse me; tell me the reason!
With what fault am I tainted, on account of which you are ready to curse me? / I am a Daitya named Gobhila, a soldier of Paulastya, O fair one.
I live according to the conduct of the Daityas; I know unsurpassed magic knowledge; / I know the meaning of the Vedas and Śāstras, and I am skilled in the arts.
"I know all this; hear from me the conduct of Daityas: / by force I enjoy another's wealth and another's wives, not otherwise."
Listen: we Daityas now act according to the conduct of Daityas / with wise understanding; truly, truly do I speak.
Day after day we watch for the weaknesses of Brahmins; / with obstacles we bring ruin to their ascetic practice, without a doubt.
Finding an opening, O lady, we destroy [them], without a doubt. / Hear about the Brahmins, O auspicious one, [and] the sacrifice to the gods, O fair-faced one:
We destroy sacrifices—the sacrifice of dharma—without a doubt, / [yet] leaving aside excellent Brahmins and Lord Nārāyaṇa the god,
and the fortunate devoted wife of wise mind, dedicated to her husband; / keeping far away, we stand clear [of them], of this there is no doubt.
O lady, the fiery brilliance of a true Brahmin, and of the great-souled Hari, / and of a woman devoted to her husband—these the Daityas are unable to endure.
Even out of fear of a devoted wife, of Viṣṇu, and of an excellent Brahmin, / all the Dānavas and foremost Rākṣasas flee far away.
I wander over the earth in accordance with the duty of a Dānava. / Why do you wish to curse me? Consider my fault!
Padmāvatī said: / My virtue and my fair body have been utterly ruined by you alone! / I am a devoted wife, virtuous, yearning for my husband, an ascetic,
steadfast upon my path, O wicked one, [yet] ruined by your illusion. / Therefore, O villain, I will reduce you to ashes, of this there is no doubt!
Gobhila said: / If your ladyship is willing, I will explain what dharma truly is. / Listen also, O king's daughter, concerning the Brahmin who keeps the sacred fire:
He who offers oblations twice a day to the deity and does not abandon the fire-sanctuary, / he becomes a maintainer of the sacred fire and truly offers sacrifice day after day.
And I will state another matter, O fair-faced one, regarding the duty of a servant: / He who is always pure in mind, action, and speech,
who constantly carries out commands, and stands behind and before [his master]— / he is called a servant, O lady, and he partakes in merit, without a doubt.
The virtuous son who understands and protects his father, being auspicious, / and especially his mother, with his mind, body, and deeds,
for him a bath in the Bhāgīrathī occurs day after day. / But he who acts otherwise is more wicked, without a doubt.
And I will state another supreme vow, that of the devoted wife, / in speech, pure thought, and action; listen, O passionate woman:
She who day after day performs service to her husband, / who is pleased when her husband is pleased and does not abandon him even if he is angry,
who does not seize upon his faults, and who, even when struck, is pleased again, / and constantly stands before her husband in all his affairs—
she is called a woman devoted to her husband. / Even a fallen father endowed with many faults
is never to be abandoned by sons for any reason, whether he is leprous or enraged. / When sons thus serve their father and their mother,
they go to the highest world, that highest abode of Viṣṇu. / In this very way, the servants who wait upon their master,
go to the world of their lord through the grace of the master. / A Brahmin must never abandon the sacred fire; he goes to the world of Brahmā.
A Brahmin who abandons the fire is called the husband of an outcaste woman; / a servant becomes a traitor to his master by abandoning his master, without a doubt.
O auspicious one, a Brahmin must never abandon the fire, a son his father, / or a servant his master; truly, truly do I speak.
Those who abandon them and depart go to the ocean of hell. / Even if he is fallen, diseased, O lady, disabled, or leprous,
devoid of all actions, and stripped of his accumulation of wealth and possessions, / a woman must not abandon her husband if she desires welfare in this world.
A woman who, abandoning her beloved, wanders off, desiring another task here— / she is considered an unchaste woman in the world, cast out from all dharma.
When her husband has gone to another village, the woman who, out of longing, / indulges in pleasures and amorous adornment—people call her an unchaste woman.
In this way I know dharma as endorsed by the Vedas and the treatises. / When the Creator originally created Dānavas, Rākṣasas, and Pretas,
I will explain the whole reason for that here, without a doubt. / Brahmins, Dānavas, Piśācas, and Rākṣasas—
everything was proclaimed for the sake of dharma, and studied by them, O lovely one; / but the Dānavas do not grasp or practice all of it.
The Dānavas, devoid of knowledge, act contrary to prescribed rule; / and those men who depart from proper rule proceed in an improper manner.
These [beings] were created for the purpose of chastising them, not otherwise. / Those vile men who practice dharma contrary to prescribed rule—
we surely punish them with severe chastisement! / A dreadful deed has indeed been committed by your ladyship, utterly pitiless!
Having abandoned the householder's life, for what purpose have you come here? / You proclaim thus with your mouth: 'I am one to whom my husband is a deity!'
In action, that devotion to your husband is not seen in you. / For what purpose have you come here, having abandoned your husband?
Putting on amorous dress and ornaments, you stand here without shame. / For what purpose was it done, O sinful woman? Tell me, for whose sake?
You roam without hesitation, intoxicated, in the mountain forest! / You have been overcome by me, O sinful one, with severe punishment; listen:
Practicing unrighteousness, wicked woman, you came here having abandoned your husband! / Where is that devotion to your husband? Show it before me!
Your ladyship is indeed an unchaste woman, by whom her own husband was abandoned. / When a woman sleeps on a separate bed, she is considered an unchaste woman.
Between you two lies an interval of a hundred leagues! / Where is your devotion to your husband, you who act according to the conduct of an unchaste woman?
O shameless, pitiless, wicked woman, what do you say to my face? / Where is the spirit of your asceticism? Where is your fiery brilliance and strength?
Show me this very day your strength, vigour, and prowess! / Padmāvatī said: / Hear, O lowest of Asuras: I was brought here out of affection
from the house of my husband by my father. Where is any sin in that? / Not out of desire, not out of greed, not out of delusion, nor out of envy
did I come, abandoning my husband; I remained steadfast with devotion to my husband. / But by you I was utterly deceived under the guise of my husband's form!
Believing you to be the man from Mathurā, I went to meet you. / When I know you to be a master of illusions, lowest of Dānavas,
with a single roar I will turn you to ashes! / Gobhila said: / Those devoid of eyes do not see, O human woman; listen now:
Lacking the eye of dharma, how can you know me here? / When the desire arose in you toward your father's house, listen,
having abandoned meditation on your husband, you were then separated from meditation; / at that time the eye of knowledge in your heart was clearly destroyed.
How can you know me on earth, struck down as you are with respect to the eye of knowledge? / Whose mother, father, or brother? Whose kinsmen and relatives?
In every place, the husband alone is the sole refuge for a wife, without a doubt! / Having spoken thus, laughing aloud, Gobhila, the lowest of Dānavas, [said:]
There is no fear for me today; listen, O unchaste woman! / What could come of your curse? In vain do you tremble all over!
Take refuge in my home and enjoy delights after your own heart! / Padmāvatī said: / Depart, you of sinful conduct! What are you saying, pitiless one?
I remain in the state of a chaste woman, devoted to the vow of fidelity to my husband. / I will burn you, O great sinner, if you speak thus!
Having spoken thus, she sat down alone on the surface of the earth. / Seized by immense grief, Gobhila said to her:
“In your womb, O fair lady, I have successfully deposited my own seed. / From it will be born a son who will shake the three worlds.”
Having said this, that Danava Gobhila then departed. / When that wicked Danava, evil in conduct, had left,
seized by immense grief, the king's daughter wept.

2.51.m: The Brahmin woman said: / “When that evil-minded, wicked Gobhila had departed, / Padmāvatī then wept, overcome with immense sorrow.
Hearing her weeping, O best of the twice-born, / all her friends, fair-faced women, questioned that princess:
‘Why are you crying? May good betide you; tell us your deeds. / Where has that great king gone, your master of Mathurā,
by whom you were summoned saying, “beloved”? Tell us!’ / Weeping again and again, she said to them in deep sorrow—
she reported everything, which had happened as a source of disgrace. / Trembling and deeply distressed, she was brought by them to her father's house.
Then the women recounted [it] in the presence of her mother. / Hearing it, the queen then went to her husband's palace.
She told her husband that very incident concerning their daughter. / Hearing it, the king then became very grieved.
Providing a carriage and clothing, accompanied by an escort, / he sent her to Mathurā; she went to her beloved's palace.
The father and mother, O best of the twice-born, concealed their daughter's fault. / But the righteous Ugrasena, seeing Padmāvatī arrived,
rejoiced immediately, and spoke this word in turn: / ‘Without you, O lovely-faced one, I am truly unable to live.
You are of great splendor, dear to me always through virtues and good character, / by your devotion, your truthfulness, O beloved, and your qualities of regarding the husband as a deity.’
Addressing his beloved wife Padmāvatī, the lord of men, / Ugrasena, the best of kings, dallied with her.
The terrible embryo grew, a source of fear for all the world. / Padmāvatī knew the origin of that embryo
growing in her own womb, and she thought day and night: / ‘What is to be gained by the birth of this one, a destroyer of the world?
I have no need now even for this wicked son.’ / She inquired everywhere for medicine to bring about an abortion.
Procuring potent herbs day after day, that woman / made numerous attempts to cause the miscarriage of the embryo.
The terrible embryo grew, causing terror to all the worlds. / Then that embryo spoke to Padmāvatī, its mother:
‘Why do you torment yourself day after day with medicinal herbs, O mother? / Through merit lifespan increases, but through sin life is brief.
Creatures live and die by the ripening of their own karma. / Other unformed embryos perish on earth unripe;
others die as soon as born; some endowed with youth, / children, old people, and youths—all fall under the power of their lifespan.
All live and die by the ripening of karma; / herbs, mantras, and deities are merely instrumental causes, without a doubt.
You truly do not know me, what sort of being I am. / You have previously seen and heard of the mighty Kālanemi,
the great hero among the Danavas, who caused fear to the three worlds. / In the great war between the gods and asuras, I was formerly slain by Viṣṇu.
To exact that hostility, I have come into your womb. / Mother, do not undertake rash action and toil day after day!’
Having spoken thus to his mother, O best of the twice-born, he fell silent. / The mother, abandoning her effort, then fell into great sorrow.
Ten years passed, during which he continued to grow; / afterwards, the very energetic one was born, who became the mighty Kaṃsa,
by whom the worlds, the dwellers of the three worlds, were terrified, / who was slain by Vāsudeva and attained liberation, without a doubt.
Thus it has been heard by me, O beloved; and what is to be will indeed happen. / In all the Purāṇas it has been definitely related to you.
A girl staying in her father's house meets destruction in this way. / For domestic life, one should not cause infatuation for a daughter in private.
Abandoning this wicked, deeply sinful woman, be resolute! / Terrible suffering and great sin are destined to be experienced.
"O beloved, enjoy that which brings well-being in the world together with me." / The female pig said this sentence; having heard that good advice, that best of twice-born
set his mind on abandoning [me]. I was then summoned; / all my clothes and adornments were given to me; hear, O auspicious one:
“Only through your misconduct, O wicked woman who ruins the family, / has the wise Brahmin Śivaśarman, best of the twice-born, departed.
Go without a doubt to where your husband stays! / Whatever place pleases you, do according as it is destined.”
Having been spoken to thus, O noble lady, abandoned by father, mother, and family, / shameless, I quickly went away, O fair-faced one.
I did not find even a dwelling place or happiness, O fair one. / People reviled me: “This unchaste woman has arrived!”
Wandering, devoid of family honor, I departed from the country / to the holy Gurjara country, to Saurāṣṭra, the abode of Śiva.
In the city known as Vanasthala, crowded with prosperity, / hear, O lady: I was then exceedingly afflicted with hunger.
Taking an earthen begging-bowl in hand, I went about for alms. / Deeply miserable, I approached the doorways of householders.
Seeing my appearance, O lovely lady, people reviled me: / “This sinful woman has come!” and they gave me no alms.
Thus, afflicted by poverty, a collector of sorrow, / while wandering, I saw an unequaled house,
surrounded by a high wall, endowed with a hall for Vedic study, / filled with the sound of the Vedas, crowded with many Brahmins,
abounding in wealth and grain, adorned with female and male servants. / That delightful house, radiant as Lakṣmī, was entered [by me].
That house, auspicious on all sides, belonged to that very Śivaśarman. / Then, afflicted by distress, Sudevā said: “Give alms!”
Śivaśarman, best of the twice-born, then heard the cry for alms. / To his wife named Maṅgalā, fair-faced, the very form of Lakṣmī,
the righteous and wise Śivaśarman, smiling, said to her: / “This frail woman has arrived, come to the doorway for alms.
Calling her, my dear, give her food, O fair one.” / Filled with supreme compassion on knowing that I had come,
Maṅgalā said to her husband: “My beloved, I will give food.” / Having said this to her husband, Maṅgalā, full of auspiciousness,
fed me, very weak as I was, with sweet food again. / That righteous, great sage Śivaśarman said to me:
“Who are you who have come here? Or to whom do you belong, wandering the world? / For what purpose do you wander everywhere? Tell me before me.”
Hearing those words of the great-souled husband, / my husband was then recognized by his voice by me, a sinful woman.'
When I saw my husband, I bowed my head in shame. / Mangalā, whose limbs were entirely lovely, said this to her husband:
"Tell [me], who is this woman who is embarrassed upon seeing you? / Please tell [me], who will this [woman] be?"

2.52.m: Śivaśarman said: / "O Maṅgalā, listen to my words if you ask now. / Learn the reason for which you have asked, O fair-faced woman.
Indeed, this wretched woman has now arrived disguised as an ascetic. / She is the daughter of the brahmin Vasudatta, O lovely-eyed woman.
Named Sudevā, she was always my beloved wife, O auspicious one. / For some reason, she abandoned the country and has come here.
She was burned by sorrow and by separation from me, O fair-faced woman. / Recognizing me, she has come to your house disguised as an ascetic.
Knowing this, O auspicious woman, a splendid hospitality should be offered / by you without doubt, if you desire what is very dear to me."
Having heard the word of her husband, the exceedingly auspicious Maṅgalā, to whom her husband was a deity, / was seized with great joy of her own accord.
That devoted wife provided for me a bath, clothing, and food, / along with ornaments studded with gems and gold, O fair-faced woman.
"Indeed, I was adorned, O auspicious woman, by that very one desiring [to please] her husband. / By her I was honored, O lady, with baths, respect, and meals.
I was honored by my husband, O lady, [yet] an endless sorrow arose / exceedingly sharp within my heart, destroying all my life-breaths.
I saw honor shown to her, and likewise the sorrow that resided within myself. / A dreadful anxiety arose in me, by which my life-breaths departed:
'An auspicious word was never spoken by me, a sinner, / to this best of brahmins, while committing evil deeds.
Washing of the feet was never done, nor massaging of the limbs; / privacy was never granted by me to that great-souled man.
How shall I, determined in sin, converse with him?' / That very night I fell there into an ocean of sorrow.
While thinking thus, my heart burst. / Then my life-breaths departed, abandoning my body, O fair-faced woman.
Then the messengers of Dharmarāja arrived there: / valiant, dreadful, cruel, wielding maces, discs, and swords.
Bound by them with chains of firm fetters, O highly fortunate woman, / I was taken to Yama's city by them, weeping and deeply distressed.
Struck with mallets, tormented along an impassable path, / and rebuked, I was ushered by them there before Yama.
I was looked upon with anger by the great-souled King Yama; / I was cast into a heap of live coals, cast into an accumulation of hells.
Having fashioned a man of iron heated by fire, / it was hurled onto my chest because of cheating my own husband.
Deeply tormented by various pains, scorched by the fires of hell, / I was cast into a vat of oil, and onto hot gruel-like sand.
Cut to pieces by sword-leaves, swept along by the Vaitaraṇī river, / and thrown onto thorny Śālmali trees by that great-souled one,
I fell into pus, blood, and feces teeming with worms. / Thus I was cast into all the hells, O princess,
intensely painful hells, by that very great-souled one. / I was ripped apart with saws and beaten heavily with spears.
Cast down into still other hells, O princess, / I was thrown into womb-pits and plunged into a crisis of suffering.
Cast down into hells by that Dharmarāja, / I entered the womb of a bat and experienced dreadful suffering.
I entered the womb of a jackal, and then entered the womb of a bitch; / I went to that of a hen, of a female cat, and indeed to the womb of a female mouse.
Thus was I cast by Dharmarāja into particular wombs, / into sinful wombs, and afflicted in all kinds of births.
By him I was made a sow upon the earth, O princess. / In your hand, O highly fortunate woman, are numerous holy waters.
Sprinkled with that water by you, O woman of excellent complexion, / my sin has departed, O lady, by your favor, O beautiful one.
Through your very power and merit, knowledge has arisen in me, O fair-faced woman. / Now deliver me, who have fallen into the distress of hell.
If you do not deliver me, O lady, I shall again go to dreadful / hell, O highly fortunate woman; protect me who am an heir to sorrow.
I have gone [astray] through sinful disposition; I am wretched and without refuge." / Sudevā said: "What virtuous deed arising from merit have I done, O auspicious one,
by which I might deliver you? Tell me that now." / The sow said: "This king is highly fortunate, an Ikṣvāku and descendant of Manu.
He is Viṣṇu, full of great wisdom; and you are Śrī, not otherwise. / You are a devoted wife, highly fortunate, intent on fidelity to your husband.
You are a faithful wife always, O auspicious one, dear and embodying all holy waters; / you, O lady, continually embody everything and are made of all the gods.
You alone in the world are a great devoted wife, beloved of the king, / by whom, by your ladyship, her husband is served day and night."
“Give me the merit of even a single day, O fair-faced one, / of the service done to your husband, if you wish to do me a favor.
You are indeed my mother and my father; you are my eternal teacher. / I am a sinful woman of evil conduct, false, and devoid of knowledge.
Deliver me, O noble lady; I am terrified of the beatings of Yama.” / Sukalā said: Having heard what was said by her thus, looking at the king at that time,
“What shall I do, O great king? What is this beast saying?” / Ikṣvāku said: “This wretched, miserable woman who has entered a sinful womb, O auspicious one,
deliver her with your own merits! Great welfare will come to pass.” / Addressed in this way, the excellent woman Sudevā, of charming auspiciousness,
said: “The merit of one year is given to you by me, O fair-faced one!” / At that very instant, by the words spoken by that lady,
she became endowed with beauty and youth, adorned with divine garlands; / and possessing a divine body, she arose enveloped in flames of splendor.
Rich in the splendor of all ornaments, and adorned with various gems, / she took on a divine form, anointed with celestial fragrant perfumes.
Mounted on a celestial chariot, that virtuous woman went into the sky. / Then she, bowing low with bent neck, said to the queen:
“May there be well-being for you, O noble lady; by your grace, O beautiful one, / freed from sin, I go to heaven, most meritorious and auspicious!”
Bowing in this way, Sudevā went to heaven, listen, O best of men! / All this that was told to you has been narrated by Sukalā.

2.53.m: Sukalā said: “Thus was dharma formerly heard by me in the Purāṇas. / Bereft of my husband, how shall I, resolved on sin, enjoy pleasures?
Without that beloved one, how may I maintain life in my body?” / Viṣṇu said: Having thus spoken of the supreme dharma, the unexcelled devotion to a husband,
those female friends, excellent women, were filled with great joy / upon hearing the supreme, meritorious dharma that grants the ultimate goal to women.
They praised that noble Sukalā, who was devoted to dharma. / The brahmins, all the gods, and virtuous women, O best of men,
meditate upon her because of the power of her love for her husband. / Considering her extreme steadfastness, Indra, the lord of the gods,
reflecting well upon the supreme state of Sukalā, the ruler of the immortals / [thought]: “I shall shake her resolve and love for her husband, without a doubt.”
Hastening, the ruler of the gods remembered the god Manmatha. / Grasping his bow of flowers, the fish-bannered [god] arrived.
Accompanied by his beloved Ratī, of seen and mighty strength, / making a hollow-handed gesture of reverence, he spoke to the thousand-eyed one:
“Why, O lord, have I now been remembered by you, O all-pervading one? / Let a command be given to me today with your whole heart, O bestower of honor!”
Indra said: “This Sukalā is a noble woman, devoted to the duty of fidelity to her husband. / Listen, O god of love, render excellent assistance!
Lure away this noble Sukalā, who is meritorious and auspicious!” / Having heard those words of Śakra, he then said to him:
“So be it, O thousand-eyed one! I will do it, without a doubt, / to assist you, O lord of the gods, for the sake of your amusement.
Having spoken thus, the immensely splendid Kandarpa, difficult even for sages to conquer, [said]: / “I am capable of conquering the gods, the munis, and the best of sages;
what then of a passionate woman, O god, who has no strength in her body? / For, O god, I dwell in the limbs of passionate women:
on the forehead, the breasts, the eyes, and always on the tips of the hair, / in the navel, the waist, the region of the back, the hips, the circle of the vulva,
on the lower lip, the parts of the teeth, and indeed in the armpit, without a doubt. / Thus I dwell everywhere in the limbs and minor parts of the body.
A woman is my home, O god; I dwell there always. / Remaining there, I destroy all men, without a doubt.
By nature, a woman is weak, O god; tormented by my arrows, / seeing her father, her mother, or any other kinsman or relative,
handsome and virtuous, O god, struck by my arrows, a woman / strays, there is no doubt here; she does not consider the consequences.
The vulva of women throbs, as do the tips of their breasts, O lord of gods. / There is no steadfastness, O ruler of the gods; I shall destroy Sukalā.”
Indra said: “I will become a man, handsome, virtuous, and wealthy. / For amusement, I shall agitate this woman, O mind-born one,
not out of desire, nor out of fear, nor out of greed, nor out of any [selfish] cause, / nor out of delusion, nor out of anger, truly, truly, O beloved of Rati!
How may her great truth and devotion to her husband be seen by me? / Going there, I shall test her; you will be the cause of infatuation here.”
Having thus instructed Kāma, the king of the gods went himself, / having transformed himself, handsome and virtuous on his own,
his body adorned with all ornaments, accompanied by all pleasures, / abounding in amorous play, and endowed with generosity at all times.
Where that lady, the beloved of Kṛkala, was staying, O king, / he displayed his amorous play, his form, virtue, and affection.
She did not even look at that man, the embodiment of beauty; / wherever she went, O king, there he looked at her.
With a longing mind, he gazed upon her in this manner. / The thousand-eyed one displayed amorous gestures through all emotional expressions.
At the crossroads, on the path, at the holy ford, wherever the lady went, / there, precisely there, the thousand-eyed one watched her alone.
A female messenger sent by Indra went to Sukalā. / Laughing gently, she spoke to the very noble Sukalā:
“Oh, your truth! Oh, your steadfastness! Oh, your radiance! Oh, your patience! / There is no woman with a fair face like hers in the whole world!
Who are you, O auspicious one? Whose wife will you be? / The man whose virtuous wife you are is blessed and fortunate on earth.”
Hearing her words, that high-minded woman said to her: / “Born in the Vaiśya caste, righteous-souled, loving the truth,
I am indeed the beloved wife of that wise man true to his pledge, / of the Vaiśya Kṛkala; I tell you the absolute truth.
My husband is righteous and wise, and has gone on a pilgrimage. / Since he, my husband, departed, O noble lady, at present,
listen, three full years have already passed. / Therefore I have become sorrowful without that great-souled one.
All this has been related to you, my own story. / You ask about me: ‘Who will you be?’ Tell me.”
Hearing Sukalā’s words, the female messenger addressed her again: / “You ask me thus, O good woman; I shall tell you all of that.
I have arrived near you for an important matter, O fair-complexioned one. / Let it be heard; I will declare it, and having heard it, keep it in mind.
Your pitiless husband has gone away, having abandoned you, O fair-faced one! / What will you do with him, the destroyer of his beloved?
That sinner who abandoned you, endowed with virtuous conduct, and went away— / where has he gone, O girl? Does he live there, or is he dead?
What will you do with him? In this way you grieve in vain. / Why do you waste your body, celestial and brilliant like gold?
When the age of childhood is reached, a human being does not find / any pleasure, O noble and auspicious lady, except children’s play.”
"In old age, suffering arrives; decrepitude harms the body. / In youth, enjoyment is experienced fully from pleasure, O fair-faced woman.
As long as youth remains, so long do mortals enjoy / all kinds of pleasures and the like; at his own will a man takes delight.
As long as youth remains, so long do they enjoy pleasures. / When age has passed, O auspicious woman, what will one do in youth?
When old age arrives, O lady, nothing at all succeeds. / An old person may constantly ponder, but pleasurable pursuits do not occur.
When age has passed, O girl, a dam is built [too late]. / Such would this body become when auspicious youth has departed.
"Therefore enjoy happily, and drink sweet intoxicating wine; / the arrows of the god of love burn these limbs of yours, O lovely-eyed one."
Here has arrived a man, handsome and virtuous. / He is indeed a tiger among men, omniscient, virtuous, and wealthy.
He is constantly devoted to your purpose out of affection, O woman of excellent complexion." / Sukalā said: "Childhood does not belong to the soul, nor does youth belong to life;
nor indeed does old age belong to it. It is self-perfected and grants true perfection, / immortal, undecaying, all-pervading, thoroughly perfected, and the best of all knowers.
Free of desire, it grants desires in the world and abides as the Self. / Just as the structure of a house is, so the structure of the body is perceived.
Just as the body is [formed] by the carpenter, so a mansion is [laid out] with measuring cord, / with assemblages of numerous pieces of wood and various collections of timber.
With clay and water too, one transforms it on all sides; / the wood is smeared by plasters and made variegated by painters.
First the house, measured out by the cord, attains form; / and day by day they maintain it through plastering.
Constantly shaken by the wind, the house becomes soiled. / The middle period of the house is declared to be the period of wear.
Loss of form occurs to it; the owner of the house replasters it, / and according to his wish, the owner brings the house back to good form.
That is declared to be the youth of that house, O female messenger. / But through collections of timbers over long periods of time, it goes to decrepitude.
They become displaced from their positions, and they shake at their bases and tips; / it cannot endure the weight of plaster, and it rests [only] on its support.
"Listen, O female messenger! This is described as the old age of the house: / seeing the house falling down, the master of the house abandons it.
He quickly departs to enter another house. / In the same way, mortals experience childhood, youth, and old age.
In childhood, having the form of a child, one behaves devoid of knowledge. / One adorns the body with garments and ornaments,
and with ointments, sandalwood, and other things derived from betel. / The body attains youth and becomes exceedingly beautiful.
One nourishes it externally and internally with all kinds of essences; / by means of that nourishment, it becomes well nourished.
An increase of flesh takes place through fresh and excellent essences. / The limbs, being refreshed, expand, O king!
Indeed, through these essences the various limbs assume their respective forms: / the teeth, the lips, the breasts, the arms, the waist, the back, both thighs,
the palms of the hands and the soles of the feet likewise attain growth; / indeed, through both of these they grow.
The limbs become shapely through essences and flesh. / By means of those forms, O female messenger, a mortal becomes bound by essences.
A mortal is called handsome, but by whom would he be beloved in the world? / This body, O messenger, is merely a receptacle of feces and urine.
This impure body constantly oozes, disgusting. / Why is its form praised, O fair one, which is like a water bubble?
It remains firm only as long as fifty years; / thereafter, day by day, decay surely befalls it.
The teeth become loose, and the mouth drools saliva; / one cannot see with both eyes, nor hear with both ears;
and with hands and feet one is unable to walk, O female messenger! / Afflicted by old age, the body becomes incapacitated.
Its essence dries up, withered by the heat of the fire of old age. / It becomes incapacitated, O female messenger; no beauty is perceived.
Just as a worn-out house goes to ruin, of this there is no doubt, / so the body falls into ruin in old age.
My form, which has come to be, you describe day by day in this manner. / With what form am I endowed? By whom is beauty acknowledged?
Just as a house falls into ruin, by what is that man strong? / For whose sake, O messenger, have you come? By whom does your ladyship praise him?
What did you see on my limb? Tell me now! / In this world, there is nothing lacking or superior in his limbs compared to mine, O messenger.
As you are, so is he, and so am I; of this there is no doubt. / Who does not have a form? There is no one on earth who possesses [true] form.
High trees and mountains have their end in falling, O fair one; / afflicted by time, they perish, and so do living beings—it is not otherwise.
The Self, formless yet possessing forms, is divine, all-pervading, and pure / in all immovable and movable beings, O female messenger.
The one pure [Self] resides [in them], like the single water in jars; / upon the destruction of the jars, it attains unity—you do not understand this oneness.
Upon the destruction of the body, this Self becomes of a single form. / One form has been perceived by me, residing constantly in worldly existence.
Speak thus having understood him for whose sake you have come here. / Show me something extraordinary, if you wish to enjoy [anything] here.
When one is tormented by disease and covered with phlegm, / the blood wanders from the limb, displaced from its proper site.
In all the joints of the limbs, it turns into flesh and goes within; / on one side it meets destruction, and it surely abandons its own form.
Quickly it turns into feces, and worms appear in it; / likewise, it abandons its own form, causing pain.
Listen! Afterward, it becomes swarming with foul-smelling worms; / lice or worms surely arise there, of this there is no doubt.
That worm causes an eruption and dreadful itching; / a louse produces torment and disturbs the whole body.
