Scratched with the tips of the nails, that itch is relieved; / listen, sexual intercourse is just like that, of this there is no doubt.
A mortal consumes food essences and drinks aplenty; / by that vital breath, it is carried to the seat of digestion.
Whatever food is eaten by living beings, O messenger, having gone to the seat of digestion, / all that is covered there, and the bodily wind expels the waste.
The essence that constitutes the core becomes blood there; / and pure, unblemished semen goes to the seat of Brahman.
Drawn by the samāna breath and carried along by that wind, / the semen finds no resting place and moves restlessly.
Indeed, in the skulls of living beings there are five worms: / these two at the roots of the ears, and then in the place of the eyes;
they have the size of a little finger, with red tails, O messenger, / and with the color of butter, but black tails, of this there is no doubt.
Hear from me their names also spoken, O gentle one: / Piṅgalī and Śṛṅkhalī are the names of the two worms at the roots of the ears;
Capala and Pippala are the two at the tips of the nostrils; / and Śṛṅgalī and Jaṅgalī, two others, reside inside the eyes.
There are one hundred and fifty such worms, of this there is no doubt; / all of them reside in the forehead, having the size of a mustard seed.
All these cranial diseases produce deformities, of this there is no doubt. / Two hairs exist in his mouth; listen, O female messenger!
Know that the destruction of living beings occurs at that very moment, of this there is no doubt. / Even when residing in its own place, in the mouth of the progenitor,
that semen falls in the form of essence, of this there is no doubt. / He drinks the semen through the mouth, and because of that he becomes intoxicated.
And in the region of the middle of the palate, it moves restlessly. / The channels called Iḍā, Piṅgalā, and Suṣumṇā are located there.
Even with great strength, inside that cage of the network of channels, / the itch of lust arises, O messenger, for all living beings.
The penis of the male twitches, and so does the vulva of the female, O messenger. / Then the woman and man, deeply intoxicated, enter into union.
The rubbing together of body with body is produced by sexual intercourse; / for just a moment there is pleasure in the body, and then the itch returns just as before.
Everywhere, O messenger, such an occurrence is seen. / Go to your own place; there is nothing extraordinary here.
There is nothing extraordinary that I would ever do, of this there is no doubt."

2.54.m: Viṣṇu said: / Addressed thus by that Sukalā, the female messenger then departed. / Having deliberated upon what had been concisely spoken, Purandara,
considering the meaning of her words endowed with truth and righteousness, / her boldness, firmness, and her true knowledge, Purandara [reflected]:
"Who indeed among women on the surface of the earth would speak like this— / words united with the nature of yoga and washed by the waters of propriety?
This illustrious woman is pure, the very embodiment of truth, of this there is no doubt; / she would be capable of bearing the burden of the entire three worlds!"
Having reflected on this matter, Jiṣṇu said to Kandarpa: / "I shall go with you to see that beloved of Kṛkala."
Manmatha, proud of his strength, answered the thousand-eyed one: / "Let us go there, O lord of gods, where that devoted wife stays."
"Her pride, her prowess, her strength, her courage, and her true devotion as a faithful wife— / having gone there, I will destroy them; how insignificant is she, O lord of the gods?"
Having heard the words of Manmatha, the thousand-eyed Indra said: / "O Ananga, listen to you who speak so boastfully in vain!
She is steadfast through the power of truth, firmly established by righteous deeds. / Sukalā is truly invincible; your virility will not prevail there."
Having heard this, then Manmatha, enraged, said to Indra: / "The power of the sages and of the gods was destroyed by me."
How trifling is her strength that you speak of to me? / While you watch, O lord of the gods, I shall ruin that woman.
Just as fresh butter turns liquid upon seeing the heat of fire, / so I will melt her by my own form and radiant power.
Go there, a great deed is now certainly at hand. / Why do you disparage my splendor, which destroys the three worlds?"

Viṣṇu said: / Having heard the word of the mind-born Kāma, [Indra said,] "I know she is unattainable to you, O Kāma— / she whose body is virtuous, rousing her courage, pure through merit, following a path of great virtue.
Let me see your fierce prowess when you go hence with your bow." / Then with him, along with Rati and the female messenger, he went again to that devoted wife.

[She was] alone, exceedingly virtuous, dwelling in her home, absorbed in meditation on her husband's feet, / just as a noble yogi, directing his mind, would make it free from conceptual wavering and not imagine anything.
Then, to bewilder the virtuous woman, the high-souled fish-bannered Kāma and Purandara / assumed a wondrous form endowed with endless splendor, adorned in blue and full of delights.
Seeing that noble man moving about gracefully in such a state of desire, / the wife of the noble vaiśya thought him endowed with beauty and appreciative of virtues.
Just as water resting on a lotus petal acquires the fame of a pearl, / even so the naturally truthful disposition of that devoted wife arose [unaffected].
"Previously, a female messenger was sent by him to me, a young woman, praising his virtues; / and this playful form of his in many aspects reveals all of his inner desire to me.

Considering that my own time has come powerfully, this truly vile man has approached with solitary virtues; / yet, accompanied by Rati, how could he live once crushed by the weight of the stone of truth?
Even if this beloved embraced my feelings, how could he survive, however intelligent he might be? / For my body is instantly empty, devoid of motion, almost like a corpse.

The citizens of the village that is the body have vanished, having taken up the activity known as great agitation; / yet Kāma has brought my dear husband's radiant appearance, equal to the supreme, to its peak.
When, though dead, the powerful one full of joy dances before his own eyes, / he who desires to enjoy me must thus speak wondrous things to him."
Having reflected thus, that great chaste woman, her consciousness firmly bound with the rope called truth, / entered her own house in order to understand his intention with restraint.

2.55.m: Viṣṇu said: / Knowing her intention, the king of gods said to Kāma standing before him: / "She cannot be conquered by you, O Smara; the chaste woman is fully armored with meditation that is the truth.
Taking the bow called righteousness in her hand, and the excellent arrow named knowledge, / this chaste woman stands in the battle to fight, like a hero proud of his prowess.
Through desire to win, she pursues the aim of human life, whereas you display your pride; / she is capable of conquering you in battle today; whatever must happen should be considered right here.
Formerly you were burned right here by the high-souled Śambhu; having made enmity with him, / as the fruit of that wrong deed you became bodiless, O Smara, in truth.
Just as the deed was done by you of old, O Smara, so too was the sharp fruit obtained; / you will surely attain a despicable womb, being described right here along with this virtuous woman.
Those knowledgeable men who cultivate enmity with high-souled beings in the three worlds / reap only the fruit of that evil deed, accompanied by sorrow and the destruction of their form.
Let us proclaim and depart, O Kāma, leaving this chaste woman alone; / formerly, in connection with a truthful woman, an unbearable sinful result was obtained by me.
You yourself know this history, how I was cursed by Gautama / and had the testicles of a ram, while you, leaving me behind, departed.
Incomparable is the power of the splendor of chaste women; neither the creator nor the sun can endure it. / May this contemptible form protect [us]; of old, Anasūyā was cursed by the sage.
By stopping the swift sun from rising, blazing as it was with radiance, / she averted her husband's death resulting from the curse of Māṇḍavya and Kauṇḍinya.
By that truthful, devoted wife, beloved of Atri, the triad of gods was reduced to her sons; / have you not heard of it of old, O Manmatha? Faithful women endowed with refinement always prevail.
She named Sāvitrī, daughter of Dyumatsena [or father of her spouse], brought back her taken beloved / from Yama right here, the noble son of Aśvapati; thus has the power of chastity been heard.
Who would touch the flame of fire? Who, having tied a heavy stone around his neck with his arms, / would foolishly swim across the ocean? Or who can subdue a chaste woman free from passion?"
When these words full of prudent counsel were spoken by Indra to instruct Kāma, / having heard those words, the dolphin-bannered [god of love] then spoke to the lord of gods:
Kāma said: / "I have come at your command; yet abandoning courage, friendship, and masculine purpose, / you speak to me to that end, making me appear devoid of strength and full of fear.
If I turn back with confused mind, O lord of gods, my fame in the world will be ruined; / without honor I would become an object of ridicule, and everyone will say that I was defeated by a woman.
The hosts of gods and demons, and the foremost sages engaged in austerities who were defeated by me before, / will now laugh at me: 'This terrible Manmatha has been conquered by a woman!'
Therefore, I will go along with you; her strength and pride, O lord of gods, / and her radiance and courage I will destroy; why are you afraid in this matter, O Śakra?"
Having thus addressed the lord of the gods, taking his bow together with an arrow of flowers, / he spoke to Krīḍā standing before him: "Assuming an illusion, you must go!
To Sukalā, the very pure wife of the vaiśya, steadfast in truth, knowing righteousness, appreciative of virtues, / go hence and carry out the assigned task as an ally; listen, dear friend!"
Having addressed Krīḍā, the mind-born god then called Prīti, who was standing beside: / "A duty of yours is my supreme duty; permeate her with tender affections!
So that this fair-eyed woman, seeing Indra, will follow him with affection, / bring her under control by various powers and words of praise; listen, dear friend!"

"O friend, go quickly, prepare an illusion-filled place possessing the appearance of the Nandana garden, / furnished with flowers, prominent with fruits, resounding with the cries of cuckoos and bees."
Summoning the hero Makaranda, an elixir endowed with sweet qualities, / along with the wind and the others engaged in their own tasks, and having dispatched Kama again,
Having thus instructed his great army, which bewilders the three worlds, Kama / set out together with the king of gods to bewilder that noble, chaste woman in this manner.

2.56.m: Viṣṇu said: / When Manmatha, along with the lord of gods, had set out to destroy her truth, / Satya then spoke to Dharma regarding Sukala:
"Behold, O Dharma, O greatly wise one, the scheming of Manmatha / against your purpose, my own, and that of the noble Merit.
I am sending forth the great site, dwelling-shaped, an arising of happiness, / named Satya, Supriya, and Sudeva—an excellent house.
Going there, this Kama of heedless mind might destroy it; / he has taken the form of an enemy and is utterly wicked toward us, no doubt.
The husband rich in austerities, the brahmin, the noble and devoted wife, / and the truly upright king, O Dharma, are without doubt my dwellings.
Where I am nourished with growth, there indeed is your dwelling; / merit arrives there and plays together with faith.
Forgiveness endowed with tranquility comes to my abode, / as do truth, self-restraint, compassion, and benevolence.
One endowed with wisdom, free from greed, is where I dwell; / a pure nature is there too, and these are my kin.
Non-stealing, non-violence, and forbearance, as well as prosperity, / have come into my house; hear of its blessedness, O Dharmarāja!
Service to elders, Viṣṇu accompanied by Lakṣmī, / and the gods headed by Agni surely enter my house.
He who reveals the path to liberation, endowed with the radiance of knowledge— / with all these I reside among chaste women and among the righteous.
In all these virtuous ones who are my dwelling-places, / even with the family I have described, I constantly dwell together with you.
Those beings of virtuous form were made into my houses by Brahmā; / O fortunate one, I roam about at will in sport.
And Īśvara, the master of the world, three-eyed and bull-mounted, / abides in my house in his true form together with Śivā.
That very essence of worldly existence, the lordly abode in the form of a house, / the dwelling named Śaṅkara, has indeed been destroyed by Manmatha.
Relying on Menakā, this Kama previously conquered / the noble Viśvāmitra who was practicing excellent tapas.
The chaste and devoted Ahalyā, Gautama's auspicious beloved, / was displaced from noble truth by that wicked Manmatha.
The sages who know the true dharma, and various devoted wives— / all these who are my houses have been burned by the fire of desire.
Difficult to restrain, unbearable, pervasive, cruel toward the truthful, / he constantly watches me: 'Where does Satya abide?'
Knowing me, he arrives with arrows in hand, holding a bow; / that wicked one, with fires of various names, would destroy my house.
Cruel traces of sin and other things that rely on hypocrisy— / all of those, harmful to wisdom, enter the house of truth.
Accomplished by that deceit with false commanders of the army, / the wicked one, with malignant weapons, would cause the house to fall and crush it.
That wicked, mighty-powered Manmatha strikes me thus; / burned by his splendor, I surely go into emptiness.
I desire a new house called woman, with husband and king; / this auspicious, blessed beloved of the meritorious Kṛkala—
The wicked one has undertaken to burn that house of mine named Sukalā; / here comes this mighty thousand-eyed [Indra] accompanied by Kama.
Because of lust, why does he not remember what happened before? / Through his liaison with Ahalyā, he was made to bear a ram's testicles.
Having seen the sage's power and because of violating a true woman, / the king of gods was ruined there through the fault of desire.
He suffered a dreadful curse, filled with great sorrow; / yet toward this beloved of Kṛkala, Sukalā, who walks in righteousness,
This thousand-eyed [Indra], joined with Kama, has risen to destroy her; / act in such a way that Kama does not come with Indra.
O Dharmarāja, greatly wise one, you are the best among the intelligent." / Dharmarāja said: "I shall diminish Kama's splendor, and also cause his death.
I have seen one expedient; let him see it right here. / And this Wisdom, highly intelligent, roaming in the form of a bird,
Let her proclaim her husband's auspicious arrival from the sky by her call; / for through the power of an omen and through the husband's arrival,
She will not be ruined by the wicked, and will be steady-minded, no doubt." / Sent by him, Wisdom went to Sukalā's house.
Making a loud cry, she appeared as if seen by the gods; / Wisdom was then worshipped and honored with incense, lamps, and other offerings.
Sukalā asked a brahmin: "What does she say to me?" / The brahmin said: "She speaks of the arrival of your husband, O fortunate one, be steady;
Within seven days he will arrive, not otherwise."
Having thus heard the very auspicious word, she was suddenly filled with joy: / that one virtuous husband who knew dharma, indicated indeed by an omen, had arrived.

2.57.m: Viṣṇu said: / Krīḍā, having assumed the form of a chaste woman, took command and went to the house of the beautiful, devoted wife; / having arrived there, that blessed one who possessed the nature of truth addressed her with respectful words.
Worshipped with most virtuous words, that Krīḍā laughed and spoke to Sukalā; / an answer following illusion, bewildering everyone, yet endowed with the measure of truth:
"My husband too was powerful, appreciative of virtues, steadfast, learned, and dignified; / abandoning me, a most sinful one, my most righteous lord, of glorious fame, departed; hear,
Having heard all that Sukalā spoke with virtuous words out of a woman's nature, / Krīḍā, considering her to be of completely pure disposition, said: 'Why has your lord departed today, O fair one,
Abandoning your truly lovely form? Tell me everything about your noble husband; / intent on meditation, she does everything; having assumed the form of a friend, she has come to my house.'
Krīḍā said: / "Hear this true account of the nature of my husband's life: / I am his beloved, ever attached to him, and whoever he desires, I conciliate toward him.
Following the very auspicious word of the noble husband, intent on meditation, I do everything; / with solitary virtue, suitable to his qualities, alone in serving him here, O lady.
This ripening of my past actions is now taking effect, / since my husband has left me, unfortunate as I am, and gone.
O friend, I cannot bear my life or my own body; / how can pitiless women live a good life when separated from their husband?
Beauty, adornment, good fortune, happiness, and prosperity—nothing else— / for the husband is sung in the scriptures as the great fortune of women."
Having heard everything that was spoken by Krīḍā at that time, / perceiving her intention to be true, she believed what was spoken then.
Trusting [her], the fortunate Sukalā, who regarded her husband as her deity, / again spoke to her all the words following her own actions.
She briefly related her own previous story: / how her husband had departed on a pilgrimage, devoted to acquiring merit,
and her own grief, which was very genuine, and her ascetic practice, O wise woman. / That chaste wife, having been enlightened and consoled by Krīḍā,
Sūta said: / Once, Krīḍā said to Sukalā: / “Friend, behold this delightful forest, adorned with heavenly trees!
There is a supreme holy place there, destroying sins, / and adorned with canopies of various creepers and lovely flowers.
We two must also go for the sake of merit, O fair-faced woman!” / Having heard [this], Sukalā then went with her by [her] deceitful power.
She entered the celestial forest resembling the Nandana garden, / endowed with blossoms of all seasons, echoing with hundreds of cuckoos,
resounding with the very sweet humming of bees, / and crowded with the holy calls of chirping sacred birds,
shining with sandalwood and other trees, and with fragrances, / fully endowed with all pleasures, [created] by Mādhava in the spring.
Indeed, it was created for the delusion of Sukalā alone. / Accompanied by her, she entered that forest which was the source of all things.
She saw that bliss-giving, sacred [forest], not perceiving its illusory nature. / Beholding the heavenly forest together with her, O ruler of people,
Śakra too arrived there, shining in divine form. / Arriving together with that female messenger, Kāma came there.
Having become the master of all pleasures, agitated by amorous sport, / addressing Kāma, he spoke: “Here is that Sukalā arrived!
Strike her who stands before Krīḍā, O noble one! / Having devised an illusion, she has been brought by Krīḍā into your presence.
Show your prowess this very day, if you have any; act with resolve!” / Kāma said: / “Display your own clever form endowed with charm,
so that I may strike her with my five arrows, O thousand-eyed one!” / Indra said: / “Where is your prowess, fool, with which you mock the world,
that, relying upon my support, you now wish to fight?” / Kāma said: / “My form was taken away previously by that god of gods,
the trident-bearing Mahādeva; I have no body. / When I wish to strike a woman, listen now [how I act]:
relying upon the body of a man, I show my form. / Or, O thousand-eyed one, to [strike] a man, I resort to the form of a woman.
When a previously seen woman constantly contemplates that very [man], / or when a man constantly meditates upon the form of a woman,
then, relying on the unseen [affection], I madden the man. / In like manner do I certainly madden a woman through [his] form, without a doubt.
From remembrance (saṃsmaraṇa), my name has become Smara, O lord of gods! / Having seen her, I take recourse to the material form of such a body.
By the radiance of its own splendor, the relationship of victim and tormentor arises. / Relying upon a woman's form, one may utterly delude a steadfast man;
relying upon a man's form, I arouse a noble woman. / I am formless, O Indra; [hence] I must take recourse to our [chosen] form.
Relying upon your form, I shall win her as desired.” / Having thus spoken to the king of gods, the flower-armed one,
the friend of Mādhava, entered the body of that great-souled one.
Eager to strike that virtuous and holy wife of Kṛkala, / the flower-armed one stood ready, eyeing her body as a target for his arrows.

2.58.m: Viṣṇu said: / Directed by Krīḍā, Sukalā, the slender-bodied wife of the merchant, having entered the forest, / saw the entire captivating thicket and asked that very friend, being a chaste woman:
“This foremost, most sacred, and celestial forest, delightful to the mind, O friend, / perfected by all excellent desires—whose is it?” Sukalā asked that friend with joy.

Krīḍā said: / “This forest is endowed with heavenly virtues, reflecting the nature of perfected beings; / filled with flowers and yielding desired fruits, behold all that belongs to the crocodile-bannered [god]!”
Then, having heard these words, filled with great joy, / and having observed the grand conduct of that wicked Kāma,
she smelled that fragrance being carried by the wind. / By its very nature, the wind blows endowed with fragrance;
his arrow enters the nostrils easily and sportively. / Yet that fair-faced woman did not take in the scent of the flowers,
nor did that great chaste woman relish the delicious savors. / That playful companion of the love-god was defeated.
Ashamed, turning his face away, he fell to the ground with drops of juice; / produced from fully ripened fruits and adorned with flower-clusters,
the sap fell to the earth in the form of drops, conquered by her. / The nectar, very dejected, having fallen from the fruit to the earth,
was devoured by flies, just as a dead body [is devoured] on a battlefield. / Being devoured by flies, it flowed away in a stream.
It flowed away very slowly, and the birds laughed at him; / they flitted about with various calls filled with joyous delight.
The birds perched on the trees in the middle of the forest rejoiced. / Indeed, he was defeated by Sukalā and took to a downward path.
Approaching joyfully, Rati, the wife of Kāma, went and smilingly said to Sukalā: / “Hail to you! Welcome indeed, auspicious lady! Delight yourself affectionately in this pleasing sight!
Your spotless beauty is desired even by the great-souled Indra. / Tell me whatever you desire, and I will bring it, without a doubt.”
Sūta said: / Seeing those two women speaking and hearing their eloquence, she said: / “My wise husband has gone, taking my love (rati) with him.
Where my husband stays, there I am united with my husband; / there lies my desire and my joy; this body here is without support.”
Having heard what was said, both Rati and Prīti felt ashamed. / Feeling embarrassed, those two went to where the mighty Kāma was.
They spoke to that great hero who had entered Indra's body, / that mighty one drawing his bow, aiming his glance [at her]:
“She is invincible, O very wise one! Abandon your prowess! / She longs only for her husband; the fortunate one is ever devoted to her husband.”
Kāma said: / “If the form of this great-souled Indra is seen by her, / O goddess, then I shall strike her, without a doubt.”
Then the king of gods, assuming a disguise, of magnificent beauty, / was quickly followed by her with supreme playfulness.
Surrounded with every luxury, adorned with all ornaments, / wearing celestial garlands and garments, and anointed with celestial fragrances,
he arrived together with that Rati to where that woman devoted to her husband was, / and addressed the fortunate, truthful Sukalā:
“Previously, a female messenger was sent by me affectionately to your presence; / why do you not respect me, auspicious lady, who have come here loving you?”
Sukalā said: / “May you be blessed! I am protected by the noble sons of my husband; / even though alone, with their help I have no fear of anyone.”
And protected everywhere by heroic sons possessing human form, / I am not at liberty to speak, being engaged in his service.
In the twinkling of an eye, O intelligent one, / why do you not feel ashamed, seeking to sport with me?
Who are you that have come here, fearless even of death? / Indra said: / Indeed, I see you thus arrived in the middle of the forest;
moreover, heroic sons of your husband were mentioned by you. / How may I see them? Show them before me!

Sukalā said: / Having installed truthful speech as ruler over his own entire group, along with those named steadfastness, mind, course, and intellect, / the great-souled one, whose entire dharma is unshakable, ever vigilant, whose nature is dharma strong against Kama, has constantly protected me.

Thus Dharma always protects me with virtues of self-restraint and purifications; / see Truth arrived before me, accompanied by peace and forbearance,
And Intellect is exceedingly mighty, of far-reaching fame, who never releases me; / I am bound by firm bonds born of his virtues, and thus he has approached my presence.
All these, beginning with Truth, have now been made to guard me; / all of them—gain of dharma and others, self-restraint, intellect, and valour—
truly protect me in this manner. Why do you solicit me by force? / Who are you that, having become fearless, have come along with a messenger?
Truth, dharma, merit, and also powerful knowledge and others— / these companions of my husband protect me in the house.
Ever endowed with protection, devoted to self-restraint and peace, / not even the lord of Śacī himself is able to conquer me.
Even if the mighty Manmatha himself comes, / I am always armoured by Truth, by Sātyaki alone, not otherwise.
His arrows will become useless, there is no doubt. / Thus the great warriors, Dharma and the others, will slay you.
Go far away! Flee! Do not stay here now! / If you stay when forbidden, you will be turned to ash.
If you look upon my form without my husband, / just as fire burns wood, so shall I burn [you], not otherwise.
Having heard this, the thousand-eyed one [spoke] to Manmatha's face: / 'Look at her virile valour! Fight with your own virile powers!'
Just as they had come, so all of them, afflicted by the fear of a great curse, / then departed, O great king, Indra and the others, each to his own place.
When all of them had gone, that faithful wife, Sukalā, / endowed with merit, returned to her home by meditating upon her husband.
O king, that woman whose deity was her husband reached her home, / which was endowed with merit, composed of all sacred places, and composed of all sacrifices.
